findings.problem: fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap() panics when the file does not exist, is unreadable, or the path is too long. This is the primary entry point for external input and must never abort the process.
findings.failure_mode: An absent or inaccessible sensor file crashes the entire consumer process instead of returning a typed I/O error that a caller can retry, log, or surface.
findings.fix: Return Result<Vec<Reading>, io::Error> (or a domain error enum) and propagate with ? instead of unwrap().

findings.problem: parts[1].parse::<u32>().unwrap() panics on three failure modes: index-out-of-bounds if the line has fewer than two commas, parse failure if the value field is not a valid integer, and the subsequent lossy as u16 truncates any value above 65535 silently.
findings.failure_mode: A single malformed CSV line (missing field, non-numeric value, or value > 65535) crashes the entire load_readings call, losing all previously parsed readings and corrupting caller state.
findings.fix: Use parts.get(1).ok_or(Error::MissingField) and parse with map_err(Error::ParseValue). Use checked_into::<u16>() or checked_cast instead of as u16 to reject values outside range with a typed error.

findings.problem: parts[1] and parts[2] use direct indexing into the Vec produced by split. If a line has fewer than two or three comma-separated fields, IndexOutOfBounds panics. Line 20 also indexes parts[2] for flags.
findings.failure_mode: Malformed lines with fewer than three fields abort the entire batch load instead of producing a per-line parse error the caller can skip or retry.
findings.fix: Replace parts[1] and parts[2] with parts.get(1).ok_or(Error::MissingField) and parts.get(2).ok_or(Error::MissingField). Handle the third field as optional with a default empty flags vec.

findings.problem: load_readings allocates freely per line: a Vec<String> for split parts, multiple String allocations for trim/to_string on each field, and a Vec<String> for flags per Reading. The function signature returns Vec<Reading> which itself allocates a Vec on the heap. No allocation budget, no try_reserve, no capacity hint exists.
findings.failure_mode: A large sensor file or adversarial input with many fields per line triggers unbounded heap allocation, potentially OOM-killering the process or causing tail-latency spikes from allocator contention.
findings.fix: Add a max_lines and max_fields_per_line parameter. Use try_reserve on the output Vec. Accept a caller-owned output buffer via fn load_readings_into(path: &str, out: &mut Vec<Reading>) -> Result<(), Error> or use an Iterator-returning shape to defer allocation.

findings.problem: println!("loaded {}", parts[0]) is a side-effecting I/O call inside the map closure. It executes for every line including lines that will later fail to parse, and it couples the pure data-loading logic to console output. This is hidden Actions inside what should be Calculations.
findings.failure_mode: Logging output appears even for broken lines, the function cannot be used in headless/batch contexts without stdout interference, and the side effect prevents the function from being pure or testable without capturing stdout.
findings.fix: Remove println! from the parse path. If logging is needed, accept a callback or return parsed items that the caller logs. Use the tracing crate with a level filter instead of println!

findings.problem: as u16 is a lossy widening/narrowing cast. Values in [65536, u32::MAX] silently truncate to u16 without any overflow detection, producing incorrect sensor data without warning.
findings.failure_mode: A sensor emitting values like 70000 silently becomes 4464, corrupting downstream analytics and potentially causing silent control-system failures in safety-critical monitoring.
findings.fix: Use u32::try_into().map_err(|_| Error::ValueOutOfRange) or let value = u16::try_from(parsed).map_err(|_| Error::ValueOutOfRange) for a checked, non-lossy conversion.

findings.problem: line.split(',').map(|part| part.trim().to_string()).collect() creates a per-line Vec<String> with to_string() on every part. This is allocation-heavy iterator chaining that allocates on every single line.
findings.failure_mode: High per-line allocation rate causes allocator pressure and GC-like pauses in the loader. For a file with millions of readings this becomes a throughput bottleneck and tail-latency spike.
findings.fix: Use line.split_once or a bounded split pattern. Parse directly into the Reading fields without intermediate Vec<String>. Consider using a crate like winnow or nom for zero-allocation CSV parsing, or at minimum use line.split(',').enumerate().map(|(i, p)| match i { 0 => ..., 1 => ..., 2 => ... }) without collecting into a Vec.

findings.problem: Reading struct has no validation invariants. sensor can be empty, value is silently truncated, and flags can contain arbitrary whitespace. Invalid domain states are representable.
findings.failure_mode: Downstream code cannot assume sensor names are non-empty, values fit u16, or flags are meaningful strings. Errors propagate as silent corruption rather than explicit validation failures.
findings.fix: Make Reading a newtype with a private constructor, or derive with a validated builder. Require sensor: non-empty string. Validate value range at construction. Trim and normalize flags.

findings.problem: load_readings at 14 lines does fit within one page, but it conflates I/O (fs::read_to_string), parsing (split/trim/collect), type conversion (parse/as), and side effects (println!) in a single function with no error separation.
findings.failure_mode: The mixed concerns make it impossible to test the pure parsing logic independently of file I/O, and any change to parsing risks breaking the I/O path and vice versa.
findings.fix: Split into: fn read_file(path: &str) -> Result<String, io::Error>, fn parse_lines(text: &str) -> impl Iterator<Item = Result<Reading, ParseError>>, and keep the caller wiring them together.

findings.problem: The map closure uses .collect::<Vec<_>>() inside the iterator chain, which means each line allocates a temporary Vec even when it will immediately be discarded after extracting fields. The final .collect() allocates another Vec for the full result.
findings.failure_mode: Double allocation per line: one for the intermediate Vec<String> parts and one for the final Vec<Reading>. For large files this doubles the allocation pressure and cache footprint.
findings.fix: Replace the intermediate collect with direct indexing or enumerate-based destructuring. Return an Iterator<Item = Result<Reading, Error>> and let the caller collect once.

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists for load_readings throughput or latency on typical sensor file sizes
no profiler evidence (perf stat, flamegraph, DHAT) to establish allocation rate or cache behavior
no rust-toolchain.toml with pinned nightly; no build profile defined in Cargo.toml
no second-ring evidence (cargo asm, cargo llvm-ir, cargo llvm-lines) for any performance claims
no cargo fmt --check, clippy, or cargo test evidence was gathered
no allocation budget statement for the load_readings function under worst-case input
residual_risk: Static review only. No commands were run. The code has multiple BLOCKER violations of panic-free policy (unwrap on I/O and parse, unchecked indexing, lossy as cast), unbounded post-init allocation, hidden I/O side effects, and no validation invariants. The function as written would crash on any malformed input, any missing file, or any sensor value exceeding 65535. A remediated version with Result types, checked conversions, bounded allocation, and split I/O from parsing would need clippy, test compilation, and benchmark evidence before acceptance.
